collards-frozen-cooked-with-butter-or-ma.title: Collards, frozen, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Collard greens are a leafy cruciferous vegetable commonly used in Southern US cuisine. The frozen version is blanched quickly, then packaged with butter or margarine, which preserves the bright green color, crisp texture, and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards belong to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts.
They have been a staple in Southern cooking for centuries, often featured in "greens" dishes.
Freezing retains up to 90 % of vitamin C and most carotenoids found in fresh leaves.
The added butter enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
Collards are frequently used in diets aimed at lowering cholesterol because of their high fiber content.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and supports bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as a powerful antioxidant and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Collards supply calcium, iron, and magnesium, important for bones, blood formation, and nerve function.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to members of the cruciferous family.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added during packaging, the sodium level can be elevated; individuals with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Heat sensitivity
items.content: Overcooking can lead to loss of heat‑sensitive nutrients, especially vitamin C.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Butter or margarine increases the calorie density of the product; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat collards in a skillet with a splash of water, add them to soups, stews, casseroles, or serve as a side dish. The butter gives a creamy taste and tender texture. They pair well with rice, quinoa, beans, or as a topping for grain bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: The fruit flavored drink comes as a powder designed for quick preparation of a refreshing beverage with a high vitamin C content. The powder dissolves in water to create a low‑calorie diet drink suitable for those monitoring sugar intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The powdered format allows long‑term storage without loss of vitamins.
Vitamin C remains active after drying thanks to micro‑encapsulation technology.
The product is easy to transport and use on trips, at work, or while camping.
Sugar content is minimal; sweetness is achieved with natural sweeteners.
The drink can be prepared hot or cold, offering different taste experiences.

items.title: High vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The diet drink provides few calories, helping to maintain energy balance.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A soluble drink helps replenish body fluids, especially in hot weather or after exercise.

items.title: No artificial colors
items.content: Only natural extracts are used for coloring, reducing the risk of allergic reactions.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: The powder dissolves quickly in water without the need for special equipment.

items.title: Allergy to fruit extracts
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to flavor components.

items.title: Excessive vitamin C intake
items.content: Very high doses of vitamin C can cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Storage in high humidity
items.content: Powder may clump and lose efficacy if kept in a damp environment.

items.title: Not recommended for children under 3
items.content: Due to the risk of accidental over‑consumption of the powder.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one serving (typically 10 g) with 200–250 ml of cold or warm water, stir thoroughly until fully dissolved. Optionally add a slice of lemon or a sprig of mint for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed. After opening, use within 3 months for best quality.

sweet-and-sour-pork-with-rice.title: Sweet and Sour Pork with Rice

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet and sour pork with rice is a popular Asian dish featuring bite‑size pieces of pork coated in a thick sauce made from vinegar, sugar, soy sauce and tomato paste, served over steamed rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in China in the 19th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Traditional sauce uses pineapple juice, but many modern recipes rely on simple vinegar and sugar.
Original recipes call for pork tenderloin to keep the meat tender.
The sweet‑sour balance is considered appetizing and stimulates the palate.
It is a staple in fast‑food restaurants, yet homemade versions allow control over salt and sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6 in pork support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Heme iron from pork is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Rice supplies carbohydrates
items.content: Steamed rice offers quick‑digesting carbs that replenish glycogen stores.

items.title: Vitamin C in the sauce
items.content: When tomato paste or pineapple is added, the sauce contributes vitamin C, which boosts immunity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet‑sour sauce can be sugar‑rich, which is a concern for diabetes or weight management.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant salt, potentially raising blood pressure.

items.title: Fatty cuts
items.content: Some pork cuts are high in saturated fat; choosing leaner pieces is advisable.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should use alternative sauces.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut pork into bite‑size pieces, stir‑fry until golden, add vegetables (bell pepper, carrot), pour a mixture of vinegar, sugar, soy sauce and tomato paste, simmer 5‑7 minutes. Cook rice separately until fluffy, then serve the pork over the rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Freeze up to 1 month, portioned appropriately.
